records.our_prose: Calendula, also called pot marigold, is an easy, cheerful flower for cool weather. It is not the same plant as the marigolds you may know (those are a different plant called Tagetes). Calendula handles light frost, blooms in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and right through winter in mild-winter areas, but it fades and stops flowering in hot summer weather. The gold and orange petals are edible and add color to food, and the flowers have long been used in skin creams and salves. Plant the seeds in cool weather, snip off faded blooms to get more, and it will often drop seed and come back on its own.

records.our_prose: Calendula is not one of USU Extension's Table 1 vegetable rows, so this spring window follows the Group A (Hardy) February 15 date given to St. George's other cold-hardy, direct-sown crops. Petals open in about 55 days and are cut through May. Calendula's own heat threshold runs around 85°F, well below St. George's documented 100°F June-through-August stretch (USU Extension: Elevations for Washington County), so bloom stalls hard once summer sets in. A second direct sowing in early August, once the worst heat has broken, follows USU's general fall-gardening guidance for restarting cool-season crops (Fall Gardening in the St. George Area); the fall stand blooms from late September up to just ahead of the average November 1 first frost.

records.our_prose: The easiest way is to sow calendula seeds straight into cool garden soil (about 60°F), a quarter to half an inch deep, and cover them well because the seeds need darkness to sprout. They come up in one to two weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost and move the young plants outside. You can pinch the tops once to make plants bushier.
records.source_context: Seeds can be sown directly in the garden just before last frost date, but for earlier bloom start seeds indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before last frost. Successive sowings will provide fresh, blooming plants throughout the season.

records.source_context: Marigolds also do well with some shade during hot summers, but become leggy in too much shade. To cultivate Marigolds, you can start seeds indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and plant the seedlings or purchased starter plants directly in the garden just after the last frost date.

records.our_prose: Calendula direct-sows readily into cool soil (about 60°F) at 1/4 to 1/2 in depth; cover the seed, because light inhibits germination. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and is the simplest method in the cool shoulders. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant; calendula resents heavy root disturbance, so use cells or pots and transplant while young. Pinch once when young for bushier plants.
